The question is “How do you feel about what the kindergarten teacher said?” The respondent first gives their attitude: “I really... am very grateful.” and adds, “I didn’t expect her to care so much about our Siwon...”.
The respondent relays Siwon’s fixed line: “Siwon always says... Mom is too pitiful.” “Mom is the most pitiful person in the world.”

The respondent adds context: “When it’s just the two of us, she often says that to me...,” and follows with “I think I kind of understand what she means now.” (showing the respondent is interpreting/understanding the intent behind Siwon’s words at this moment).
The respondent summarizes Siwon’s view again: “Siwon thinks Mom is the most pitiful person in the world.” (treating “Mom is the most pitiful” as Siwon’s core judgment).
The respondent continues describing Siwon’s “comparison—avoidance” logic: if “Siwon cries,” people around will “think Siwon is pitiful,” and then “come over to comfort her.”

The respondent gives Siwon’s inferred conclusion: once people come to comfort her, Siwon will “become more pitiful than Mom” (i.e., Siwon does not want pity to shift from Mom to herself because of crying).

This narrative contains two relationship clues at the information level: first, Siwon sees “Mom” as someone who needs sympathy/protection; second, Siwon cares about where others’ sympathy is directed, avoiding gaining sympathy through crying and thus “overshadowing” Mom’s pitiful situation.

Since you have explained that the current order may “not be sorted yet,” there is room to later adjust the subject/speaker between “respondent = Choi Donggeon (dad)” and his relay of “When it’s just the two of us, she often says that to me...”: this emotional position feels more like “the person who is alone with Siwon and repeatedly hears ‘Mom is the most pitiful’,” and if the speaker is changed later, this can be used as a basis for adjustment (for now, record as presented without final identity confirmation).

The overlap of name and age pulls everything back to the beginning: she is Choi Siwon—the missing child you once tried to recover, who ultimately made it home. She tells you the case originally would not have been taken seriously; it was because you did not brush it off or just go through the motions that a ‘process that could have been ignored’ became ‘the chance to send someone home.’ When the truth lands, what you receive is not absolution but a final handoff: before your memory fades completely, finish what is not yet finished—bring this cold case to a true close.

memory.description: This is the final ending. time no longer moves forward—it collapses inward. Twelve years of blankness are uncovered: the so-called ‘Grandma,’ ‘Judge,’ and ‘Officer Jeon Gyeong’ were never separate people, but the same consciousness split into different forms to survive reality. Siwon’s case did not remain unresolved because of institutions or truth, but because one person sealed it away with lies and forgetting for twelve years. Now, all identities return to the origin, all memories snap back into place, and the person who truly needs saving is finally recognized.

After retirement, Jeon Gyeong became director of a law firm, using busyness and role change to escape the responsibility and pain from that case.
Jeon Gyeong admits: she believed the case was over and everyone was satisfied—this was the lie she left for herself.
Images and identities begin to misalign: the ‘Grandma’ on the left gradually reveals herself as Jeon Gyeong, while the ‘Jeon Gyeong’ on the right is exposed as a trapped ideology/state of mind.
Jeon Gyeong realizes: she left through lies, but another version of herself was imprisoned like a scarecrow in the wilderness of ‘unsolved’ for twelve years.
Jeon Gyeong identifies the real subject: Song Minyoung. Her sentence ended long ago, yet she remains trapped in a treatment custody facility.
Identity reveal completes: the ‘Jeon Gyeong’ on the right is ultimately revealed as Song Minyoung—she keeps switching between personas, sometimes Siwon, sometimes a police officer.
Jeon Gyeong explains: these dialogues, memories, and time aren’t fake—they are the result of Minyoung’s experiences interwoven with Jeon Gyeong’s long-running narration.
A key missing piece is named: Song Minyoung confirmed memories, narrators, and timelines, but never managed to determine who the listener was.
Final puzzle: the listener, the judge, the police, and the judged were always the same person.
Jeon Gyeong asks Song Minyoung to leave and go somewhere she can truly receive treatment, promising to accompany and help her.
Song Minyoung asks the final question: since Jeon Gyeong is no longer a police officer, why help her?
Jeon Gyeong gives the final answer: it’s the very question she once asked Siwon, and the answer has never changed.
Closing confirms: Siwon’s disappearance remained unresolved; now it’s time to settle it—not as a case, but as a life.
